blurb: A practice system for technical writing about GPUs, model training, inference, reinforcement learning (RL), systems, code and the mathematics behind them. It trains one skill at a time on your own work, across four forms: blog posts, white papers, conference papers and journal articles.

items.title: The 12-week program
items.html:
Each week trains one sub-skill. Daily drills isolate it; the weekly piece applies it to your own work; the weekly reading shows a professional doing it. The forms climb a ladder: sentence → paragraph → figure → explainer → blog → white paper → paper → submission.

The cadence (every week):

RhythmTimeWhatFeedback
Daily drill, 5 days25 minpython tools/tw.py today, then tw drilltw lint, then the drill's Done when
Weekly piece2–3 hThe piece listed for the week, in journal/tw review after 24 h, then prompts/reviewer.md
Weekly reading45 minThe exemplar for the week, with reading/protocol.mdYour reverse outline vs. the author's structure
Friday retro10 mintw stats; write one line: what I will practise next week—

Rules that make this a discipline rather than a course:

  1. Write before you read the guide. Do the drill cold, then read the principle file, then revise. The gap between the two versions is the lesson.
  2. Never edit while drafting. Timer on, write, stop. Editing is a separate session.
  3. Cool off before reviewing. 24 hours minimum. Fresh eyes read what you wrote, not what you meant.
  4. Ship on schedule. A published 70% piece teaches more than a perfect draft in a folder. Weeks 6, 8 and 12 have external deadlines; keep them.
  5. No model answers. Nobody, human or AI, writes your piece. Reviewers point at problems; you fix them.

Seed topics with facts and data from your own work are in seeds/. Use them, or bring your own (reinforcement learning (RL) experiments, training runs, systems at work); the same week structure applies.

Math in prose
Mathematics in technical writing is prose with symbols in it. Define every symbol before use, read every equation as a sentence, and say what each equation is for before you show it.

**Read:** `principles/05_math.md`. Exemplars: Paul Halmos, *How to Write Mathematics* (1970); Lilian Weng, *Policy Gradient Algorithms* (blog, 2018).

items.title:
After week 12

Keep the cadence; change the content.

- **Daily:** one drill, chosen from your weakest rubric row (`tw stats` and your review sheets tell you which).
- **Monthly:** one finished piece, rotating forms: blog, then explainer or postmortem, then white paper or paper section.
- **Quarterly:** one submission (paper, journal article, or a practitioner venue such as ACM Queue) and one talk.
- **Every piece:** a reverse outline before revising, and a 24-hour cool-off before review.

It trains one skill at a time on your own work, across four forms: blog posts, white papers, conference papers and journal articles.
items.title: Using the tools
items.html:
A practice system for technical writing about GPUs, model training, inference, reinforcement learning (RL), systems, code and the mathematics behind them. It trains one skill at a time on your own work, across four forms: blog posts, white papers, conference papers and journal articles.

It is built on deliberate practice: short daily drills that isolate one sub-skill, a weekly piece that applies it to real material, feedback you can measure, and a schedule. There are no model answers to copy. The tools find mechanical faults; rubrics, cool-off reviews and human readers judge the rest.

Quick start

Python 3.9 or later, standard library only.

python tools/tw.py start          # day 1 of week 1 is today
python tools/tw.py today          # this week's skill, today's drill, drafts ready for review
python tools/tw.py drill          # creates today's drill in journal/; set the timer it prints
python tools/tw.py lint journal/2026/2026-10-28-d01-*.md
python tools/tw.py done journal/2026/2026-10-28-d01-*.md --minutes 25

The weekly piece:

python tools/tw.py new blog atomics-cliff     # templates/blog.md -> journal/YYYY/...
# draft it; wait 24 hours
python tools/tw.py review journal/2026/....md # lint summary + rubric sheet + reverse outline
# then an outside critique without rewriting: prompts/reviewer.md
python tools/tw.py stats                      # streak, words, fix rate and rubric score per week

Other commands: tw drills (the catalogue), tw drill D17 (a specific drill), tw new KIND SLUG with KIND one of blog explainer postmortem whitepaper paper abstract adr review reading.

The weekly rhythm

TimeWhat
Daily, 5 days25 minOne drill on the week's skill
Weekly2–3 hOne piece from your own work
Weekly45 minOne exemplar, read as a writer (reading/protocol.md)
Friday10 mintw stats, and one line: what to practise next

PROGRAM.md lays out the 12 weeks: reader and claim, paragraphs, numbers, figures, mechanisms, mathematics, systems narratives, white paper, paper (two weeks), review and rebuttal, and shipping.

Phone and computer

web/ is the same program as an installable page. It works in a desktop browser and on a phone (install it from the browser menu: Install app or Add to Home screen). After the first load it keeps working offline.

python tools/build_web.py          # rebuild web/content.json after editing the Markdown
python -m http.server -d web 8765  # then open http://localhost:8765

Read the weeks, the drills and the library. Each drill has a timer and a writing box. Notes and progress stay in the browser; the ⋮ menu exports and imports them. Set Week 1 begins to the day you ran tw start, and the page picks the same drill as tw today. The journal of record is still the tw tools on your computer.

Publishing the page (GitHub → Settings → Pages → Source: GitHub Actions) puts it at https://venkatacrc.github.io/techwriter/ after a push to main.

The rules

  1. Write before you read the guide.
  2. Never edit while drafting.
  3. Cool off for 24 hours before reviewing.
  4. Ship on schedule.
  5. No model answers: reviewers point at problems; you fix them.

Map

PathWhat
PROGRAM.mdThe 12-week plan and what comes after
drills/catalog.md48 drills, each with a skill, a time box and Done when criteria
principles/Eight short guides: reader and claim, structure, paragraphs and sentences, numbers and evidence, mathematics, figures and tables, code and systems, revision
forms/What each form's reader decides and what evidence it needs: blog, white paper, paper, journal
templates/Skeletons with prompts, no prose, for every kind of piece
rubrics/1–4 scoring by form; tw review builds a sheet from them
seeds/Facts from your GPU kernels course, with sources and evidence gaps, plus slots for your RL, training and math work
reading/The reading protocol and the exemplar list
publishing/Venues, and the process from employer approval to rebuttal and revision
prompts/reviewer.mdAn AI critique prompt that quotes and diagnoses but never rewrites
tools/tw.py (the workflow) and twlint.py (the linter)
journal/Your writing: drills, pieces, review sheets

The linter

twlint.py flags filler words, hedges, weasel words, vague claims with no number, comparisons with no baseline, undefined acronyms, repeated words, long sentences and long paragraphs. It ignores code, math, URLs and front matter. Each issue is either fix (almost always wrong) or look (often fine; decide). Suppress a deliberate exception with ` on the line or the line above, and add acronyms your readers know to tools/known_acronyms.txt`.

The linter is a spell-checker for habits, not a judge of writing. A piece can be lint-clean and pointless. The rubric rows on reader, claim and evidence matter more than every lint rule together.

Measuring progress

tw stats tracks practice volume (days, streak, words, minutes) and two quality signals per week: lint fix items per 1,000 words, which should fall in the first month and stay low, and the average rubric score from your review sheets, which should rise. The best signal is outside the tools: whether readers act on what you write, and what reviewers say about it.

items.summary: Most unclear technical writing is not made of bad sentences. It is made of good sentences serving an unclear claim, written for nobody in particular. Fix those two things first; sentences come last.
items.title: 1. The reader and the claim
items.html:
Most unclear technical writing is not made of bad sentences. It is made of good sentences serving an unclear claim, written for nobody in particular. Fix those two things first; sentences come last.

Name the reader

Before writing, answer four questions about one specific reader:

QuestionWeak answerUseful answer
Who?"ML engineers""Priya, who trains ranking models in PyTorch and has never written a kernel"
What do they know?"the basics""autograd, mixed precision, profilers at the PyTorch-op level; not warps, not high-bandwidth memory"
What will they do after reading?"understand X""decide whether to fuse their attention layer, and estimate the gain"
What makes them stop reading?—"three paragraphs of GPU history before the point"

"Understand" is never the answer to the third question. Readers act: they adopt a technique, approve a budget, accept a paper, cite a result, or avoid a bug. Write for the action.

The main obstacle is the curse of knowledge (Steven Pinker's term in The Sense of Style): once you know something, you cannot easily imagine not knowing it. You skip steps that feel obvious, use your team's private vocabulary, and assume the reader saw the same plots you did. The reader card (drill D02) forces you to write down what they do not know.

State a claim, not a topic

A topic names an area. A claim asserts something a reader could disagree with and could check.

  • Topic: "This post discusses key–value (KV) cache memory management in large language model (LLM) serving."
  • Claim: "Storing the KV cache in fixed-size pages, as an operating system pages virtual memory, removes most of the fragmentation that limits batch size, which is why vLLM's authors report 2–4× higher throughput than earlier serving systems at the same latency."

The claim tells the reader what to believe, why, and how strongly. It also tells you what evidence the piece needs: a fragmentation measurement, a batch-size effect, and a throughput comparison with a fair baseline.

Tests for a claim:

  1. Disagreeable. Could a competent reader say "no"? "GPUs are important for deep learning" fails.
  2. Checkable. Could a reader, in principle, verify or falsify it? "Our approach is more elegant" fails.
  3. Sized. Does its strength match your evidence? "Always" needs a proof; "in our measurements on one GPU" needs only your logs.
  4. Owned. Is the subject your work, and the verb something it does? "We show", "the kernel removes", "the policy learns", not "we study" or "this work is about".

Activity versus contribution

Status reports describe activity: "We investigated several kernel fusion strategies and benchmarked them." Technical writing reports contribution: "Fusing the gate multiply into LayerNorm removes two of five memory passes and makes the layer 2× faster on GB200." Activity is what you did; contribution is what the reader gets. Readers do not care how hard you worked, only what is now true.

The so-what ladder

A measured fact sits at the bottom of a ladder of consequences (illustrative numbers):

  1. Decoding images on the GPU instead of in CPU workers raised GPU utilisation from 55% to 92%. (fact)
  2. So the training step is no longer bound by the input pipeline. (system)
  3. So an epoch takes 40% less wall-clock time on the same hardware. (project)
  4. So the team can run the same experiment schedule on fewer GPUs. (organisation)
  5. So input-pipeline throughput should be measured before any model-side optimisation. (field)

Different forms open on different rungs. A paper opens on rung 5 and proves rung 1. A white paper opens on rung 4. A blog post often opens on rung 1 as a hook, then climbs. Know which rung you are on (drill D03).

Before you write anything longer than a page

Write these three lines at the top of the draft, and delete them only when the piece is done:

Reader:   <one person, what they know, what they will do>
Claim:    <one sentence, disagreeable, checkable, sized>
Evidence: <the two or three things that make the claim true>

If you cannot fill in the claim, you are not ready to draft; you are ready to think, measure or outline. That is fine, and it is cheaper to find out now.

items.summary: Structure is the order in which the reader meets your ideas. The writer's natural order is chronological ("first I tried, then I found"). The reader's useful order is usually the reverse: conclusion, then the evidence that supports it, then the detail for those who want it.
items.title: 2. Structure
items.html:
Structure is the order in which the reader meets your ideas. The writer's natural order is chronological ("first I tried, then I found"). The reader's useful order is usually the reverse: conclusion, then the evidence that supports it, then the detail for those who want it.

Lead with the point

Put the answer before the reasoning. Military and business writers call this BLUF (bottom line up front); Barbara Minto's pyramid principle is the same idea, made recursive: the top of the document states the main point, each section states a supporting point at its top, each paragraph states its point in its first sentence.

Chronological outline of a post on activation checkpointing:

  1. I was training a 1.3B model and ran out of memory.
  2. I tried a smaller batch, which hurt throughput.
  3. I read about checkpointing.
  4. I implemented it and measured.
  5. It saved memory at a compute cost.

Pyramid outline of the same post (illustrative numbers):

  1. Checkpointing every second transformer block cut peak memory by 40% for a 20% slower step, which let me double the batch and finish 1.4× sooner overall.
  2. Why it works: activations dominate memory, and recomputing them is cheaper than storing them.
  3. How to choose what to checkpoint: the memory–compute trade-off per layer type.
  4. The measurements, and when it does not pay.

The first outline makes the reader wait for the point and guess what to pay attention to. The second tells them on line one, so every later section reads as support.

Chronology has one legitimate use: when the process is the content (worklogs, postmortems, tutorials). Even then, state the outcome at the start so the reader knows where the story ends.

Sections answer the reader's questions, in their order

List the questions your reader will ask, in the order they will ask them. That list is your outline. For a performance result a reader typically asks: what is faster, by how much, compared with what, why, does it hold elsewhere, what does it cost, and how do I use it. If your sections follow a different order, the reader carries open questions through the text, and loses track.

Headings

  • In blogs, explainers and white papers, headings can state claims: "Shared atomics serialise at L2" tells more than "Atomics". A reader skimming headings alone should get the argument.
  • In papers, use the conventional skeleton (Introduction, Background, Design, Evaluation, Related Work, Conclusion) because reviewers navigate by it, but make subsection headings and paragraph leads informative.
  • Never use a heading as the first sentence of a paragraph ("## Results" followed by "These are shown below"). The text under a heading must stand without it.

Signposts and transitions

A signpost tells the reader where they are going ("Two effects explain the gap: occupancy and memory coalescing. We take them in turn."). A transition tells them how the next idea relates to the last: contrast (but, however), cause (so, because), addition (also), example (for instance), concession (although). If you cannot find the right transition word between two paragraphs, the relationship is unclear in your head, and reordering may help more than rewording.

The reverse outline

The single most useful structural tool. After drafting, write one line per paragraph stating what it claims, without looking at your headings. Read the list alone. It shows:

  • paragraphs making two points (split them),
  • two paragraphs making the same point (merge them),
  • points out of the reader's order (move them),
  • points with no evidence (support or cut them),
  • a missing step in the argument (write it).

Every self-review sheet that tw review creates includes a reverse outline. Do it every time.

Length is a structural decision

Decide the length before drafting, from the form and the reader's time (see forms/). A 1,500-word post with four sections gives each about 350 words: that is three or four paragraphs per section. Knowing the budget stops one section from swallowing the piece.

items.summary: Readers process text with expectations about where information sits. Meet those expectations and the reader spends their effort on your ideas; violate them and they spend it on your sentences. The principles below come mostly from George Gopen and Judith Swan's The Science of Scientific Writing (1990) and Joseph Williams's Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace.
items.title: 3. Paragraphs and sentences
items.html:
Readers process text with expectations about where information sits. Meet those expectations and the reader spends their effort on your ideas; violate them and they spend it on your sentences. The principles below come mostly from George Gopen and Judith Swan's The Science of Scientific Writing (1990) and Joseph Williams's Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace.

Paragraphs

One point per paragraph, stated first. The first sentence (the topic sentence) states the point; the rest supports, qualifies or illustrates it. A reader who reads only first sentences should get the argument. When a paragraph makes a second point, start a new paragraph.

Length follows the point. In technical prose, 60–150 words is common. A 250-word paragraph usually holds two points; a run of one-sentence paragraphs usually means points with no support.

Sentences: what goes where

Characters as subjects, actions as verbs. Readers expect the subject to be who or what acts, and the verb to be the action. Nouns made from verbs (nominalisations) hide both.

  • Before: "The utilisation of a fused optimizer resulted in a reduction of the step time."
  • After: "The fused optimizer reduced the step time."

Keep subject and verb close. Everything between them is held in working memory until the verb arrives.

  • Before: "The data loader, which decodes JPEGs on 8 CPU worker processes and applies random crops and flips before collating each batch of 256 images, stalls the GPU."
  • After: "The data loader stalls the GPU: it decodes JPEGs on only 8 CPU worker processes, then crops, flips and collates each 256-image batch."

Old information first, new information last. The start of a sentence (the topic position) should link back to what the reader already has; the end (the stress position) should carry the new and important information. This makes sentences chain:

  • Before: "Throughput dropped by 30%. A synchronisation point was introduced by the .item() call in the logging code. The CPU waits for the GPU at every step because of it."
  • After: "Throughput dropped by 30% after we added per-step logging. The logging code calls .item(), which is a synchronisation point. At every step, the CPU now waits for the GPU to finish before it can launch the next kernel."

In the revised version, each sentence starts with something the previous one introduced (logging, then *.item()*, then synchronisation) and ends on the new fact.

Words

Use one term per concept, always the same one. In literary prose, varying synonyms is elegant. In technical prose it is a bug: if paragraph 2 says "program", paragraph 3 "block" and paragraph 4 "CTA" (cooperative thread array), the reader must wonder whether these are three things. Pick one, define it once, and keep it.

Give "this" a noun. "This is why the kernel is slow" makes the reader search backwards for the referent. "This bank conflict is why the kernel is slow" does not.

Prefer the concrete word. "Performance improved" → "step time fell from 41 ms to 29 ms". "Various optimisations" → "three optimisations: fused AdamW, CUDA graphs, and bf16 logits".

Cut words that do no work. Very, really, basically, actually, in order to, it should be noted that. The linter lists them; delete or replace each one it finds unless you can say what it adds.

Hedge once, precisely, where the uncertainty is. "It might perhaps be possible that this could help" is four hedges for one uncertainty. "On our two GPUs this helped; we have not tested other architectures" places the uncertainty and sizes it.

Rhythm

Vary sentence length. A run of long sentences tires the reader; a run of short ones reads like a list. Put the most important idea of a paragraph in a short sentence, after a longer one that sets it up.

When items are parallel (steps, options, results), make the grammar parallel too, and consider a list. When items are related causally, keep them in prose: lists hide the "because".

Active and passive

Use the active voice when the actor matters ("the scheduler evicts the oldest request"). The passive is correct when the actor is unknown or irrelevant ("the weights are stored in bf16"), and in methods sections where the experimenter is obvious. The linter flags passives for you to look at, not to remove by rule.

items.summary: Technical readers check your evidence before they believe your prose. In GPU, systems, training and reinforcement learning (RL) writing, most evidence is a measurement, and most errors are in how a measurement is reported, not in the measurement itself.
items.title: 4. Numbers and evidence
items.html:
Technical readers check your evidence before they believe your prose. In GPU, systems, training and reinforcement learning (RL) writing, most evidence is a measurement, and most errors are in how a measurement is reported, not in the measurement itself.

The five parts of a reported number

  1. Value, with precision the spread supports.
  2. Unit. "7.1" means nothing; "7.1 TB/s" means something.
  3. Baseline: relative to what? "3× faster" than which implementation, version and configuration?
  4. Conditions: hardware, software versions, shapes, dtype, batch size, dataset, and anything else that changes the number.
  5. Spread and count: how many runs, and how much they varied.

A sentence with all five (illustrative numbers): "On 8 H100 GPUs connected by NVLink, an all-reduce of 1 GiB of bf16 gradients takes 4.2 ms with NCCL 2.21 (median of 50 runs after 10 warm-up runs; range 4.1–4.4 ms), against 6.9 ms for the same all-reduce over PCIe on the same machine."

Not every sentence needs all five in-line: a setup section can state conditions once. But every number must be traceable to all five somewhere in the piece.

Ratios and percentages

Ratios are where most reporting errors live.

  • "50% faster" is ambiguous: does throughput rise 50%, or does time fall 50% (which is 2× throughput)? Report the two raw values, then the ratio.
  • "3× less memory" is unclear; write "one third of the memory" or "4.2 GB → 1.4 GB".
  • Average ratios with the geometric mean, not the arithmetic mean: the arithmetic mean of 2× and 0.5× is 1.25×, which claims a gain where there is none.
  • Report latency with the median and tail percentiles (p50, p99), not the mean; one outlier moves a mean.

Fair comparisons

Your result is only as strong as your baseline. A reviewer's first question is "did you beat a strawman?" Make the baseline strong, and say how:

  • the strongest available implementation, at its current version, with its recommended settings;
  • the same hardware, inputs, precision and batch size;
  • the same tuning effort (if you autotuned yours, tune theirs);
  • the same measurement method (warm-up, synchronisation, repetitions);
  • and state what remains unfair in your favour.

Gernot Heiser's Systems Benchmarking Crimes lists the common failures: benchmarking a subset of workloads and implying the whole, reporting only relative numbers, no indication of variance, an improper or outdated baseline, measuring at unrealistic scale, and not explaining a surprising result. Read it once a year.

Variance, seeds and significance

  • Systems measurements: report repetitions, warm-up, and the statistic used (median, minimum, mean). GPU timings vary with clocks, temperature and other tenants on shared machines; say if the machine was shared.
  • Training results: report the number of seeds and the spread across them. A one-point gain in a metric that varies by two points across seeds is not a result.
  • Reinforcement learning: variance across seeds is large and the tooling for reporting it matters. Henderson et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters (AAAI 2018), showed how seeds and implementation details change conclusions. Agarwal et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice (NeurIPS 2021), recommends interval estimates and robust aggregates such as the interquartile mean, instead of point estimates from a few runs.

Match the strength of the words to the evidence

EvidenceLanguage that fits
One run, one machine"in our run", "we observed"
Repeated runs, one setup"on this setup, the median ..."
Several setups or seeds, with intervals"across N seeds", "on average", with the interval
A mechanism you measured at each link"because"
A mechanism you inferred"we believe", "likely", and say what would test it
A proof"always", "for all"

Overclaiming is the most common reason reviewers reject a paper whose experiments are fine. Underclaiming wastes good evidence. Size the claim.

Precision

Report as many significant figures as the spread supports. If runs vary by ±3%, "7,142 GB/s" implies false precision; "7.1 TB/s" is honest. Keep raw values with full precision in a table or appendix for readers who want them.

The claim–evidence table

For any piece longer than a page, keep a two-column table: every claim on the left, its evidence on the right (measurement and where it is logged, citation, derivation, or "none yet"). Every "none yet" must be measured, softened or cut before you publish. Drill D12 builds the habit.

The classic guides are Paul Halmos, How to Write Mathematics (1970); Donald Knuth, Tracy Larrabee and Paul Roberts, Mathematical Writing (Stanford lecture notes, 1989); and, for proofs, Leslie Lamport, How to Write a 21st Century Proof (2012).

The innovations you want to write about (attention variants, optimisers, quantisation, policy gradients, scaling laws, roofline models) are explained with mathematics. Mathematical writing is prose that contains symbols, and the same rules apply: reader first, purpose first, one idea at a time. The classic guides are Paul Halmos, How to Write Mathematics (1970); Donald Knuth, Tracy Larrabee and Paul Roberts, Mathematical Writing (Stanford lecture notes, 1989); and, for proofs, Leslie Lamport, How to Write a 21st Century Proof (2012).

Say what the equation is for before you show it

A reader meeting an equation asks: why am I looking at this? Answer first.

  • Before: "Let Gt = ∑k=0∞ γk rt+k+1."
  • After: "The agent should prefer actions that lead to high reward later, not only now. We measure later with the discounted return, the sum of future rewards, each shrunk by a factor γ ∈ [0, 1) per step of delay: Gt = ∑k=0∞ γk rt+k+1."

Define every symbol, before or immediately after its first use

For each symbol give what it is, and its type, shape or unit: "Q ∈ ℝN × d, the queries for a sequence of N tokens with head dimension d". For a paper with more than about ten symbols, add a notation table. Never redefine a symbol, and never use one symbol for two things (N as sequence length and as batch size in the same paper is a real and common error).

Keep notation consistent and conventional

  • Follow your field's conventions: lowercase bold or plain lowercase for vectors, uppercase for matrices, θ for parameters, π for policies, 𝔼 for expectation.
  • Write multi-letter names upright: softmax, SiLU, clip. Italic softmax reads as a product of seven variables.
  • Match code and math when you show both: if the code says head_dim, the text says d and states once that d is head_dim.

Equations are parts of sentences

An equation is read aloud as words, so it takes the punctuation those words would need.

The proximal policy optimisation (PPO) objective clips the probability ratio L(θ) = 𝔼t[min(ρt At, clip(ρt, 1-ε, 1+ε) At)], where ρt is the ratio of the new to the old policy's probability of the action taken and At is the advantage estimate.

Note the comma after the display and the "where" clause that continues the sentence. Do not start a sentence with a symbol ("x is ..." becomes "The input x is ...").

Words, equation, words

After a displayed equation, say in words what it means and what to notice: a sign, a limit, a scaling, a special case. For the clipped objective: "When the advantage is positive, the objective stops increasing once the ratio exceeds 1+ε, so one update cannot move the policy far from the one that collected the data." This sentence is where understanding happens; the equation is only where precision happens.

Derivations: signpost every step

A derivation is an argument, not a wall of algebra. Before each step, state what it does ("expand the square", "the cross term vanishes because the noise has zero mean", "apply the chain rule through the SiLU"). A reader should be able to follow the derivation by reading the signposts alone. Move routine algebra to an appendix and keep the steps where something happens in the main text.

Check your math in the text

Show the reader the checks that build trust (drill D24):

  • Units or dimensions. If bandwidth is bytes per second and latency is seconds, bytes in flight is their product, in bytes.
  • Limiting cases. With γ = 0 the return is the immediate reward; with ε → ∞ PPO's objective becomes the unclipped policy gradient.
  • A number. Plug in a real value from your own experiment and show that the formula predicts what you measured.

Statements and quantifiers

A theorem or claim states all its assumptions ("for a differentiable policy with bounded rewards"). Use "for all", "there exists", "almost surely" deliberately. "Converges" needs a sense (in expectation? with probability one?) and a rate if you have one.

Mechanics

  • In blogs, render math with KaTeX or MathJax and check it on mobile.
  • In papers, number only the equations you refer to; refer to them as "Equation (3)" or "Eq. 3", consistently.
  • In LaTeX, use \left( \right) sparingly, \cdot for multiplication when needed, and \text{} or \mathrm{} for words inside math.

items.summary: Many readers of a technical paper look at the figures before reading a sentence, and some read nothing else. Treat each figure as the argument in miniature.
items.title: 6. Figures and tables
items.html:
Many readers of a technical paper look at the figures before reading a sentence, and some read nothing else. Treat each figure as the argument in miniature.

One message per figure

Before plotting, write the sentence the figure should prove: "Throughput grows almost linearly with batch size until 512 users, then flattens." Design the figure so that sentence is visible within two seconds. If a figure carries two messages, make two figures.

Choose the encoding from the question

Reader's questionUsually best
Which is bigger? (few items)Bar chart starting at zero, or a dot plot
How does it change with X?Line plot; log axes if X spans orders of magnitude
How does it scale?Log–log plot; a slope tells the exponent
What is the distribution? (latency, reward across seeds)Cumulative distribution (CDF), box or violin plot; never a mean alone
Where does the time go?Stacked bar or a sorted horizontal bar of components
Is it compute- or memory-bound?Roofline plot (performance vs arithmetic intensity)
Throughput versus latency trade-offThroughput–latency curve, one point per load level
Exact values to look upA table

Tables are for lookup and for exact values; figures are for patterns and comparisons.

Captions state the takeaway

A caption has three parts, in this order: the takeaway, what is plotted, and how to read it.

Figure 3. Dynamic batching raises throughput 15× at 128 clients without raising tail latency. Requests per second (left) and p99 latency (right) against the number of concurrent clients, for the same model served with and without dynamic batching on one GPU. Medians of three 5-second runs; bars show the range.

The reader of the figure alone now knows what to conclude and how much to trust it.

Make it readable

  • Label axes with quantity and unit: "Step time (ms)", not "time".
  • Label lines directly at their ends when possible, instead of a legend the eye must travel to.
  • Keep colours consistent across all figures (your method is always the same colour), and choose colourblind-safe palettes (such as Okabe–Ito or ColorBrewer qualitative sets). Use colour for categories, not decoration.
  • Show variance: error bars, bands or individual points; say in the caption what they are (standard deviation, 95% interval, min–max).
  • Do not truncate bar charts. A bar's length is its value; a bar axis that starts at 90 exaggerates a 2% difference into a 2× visual one. Line plots may zoom if the axis range is labelled.
  • Avoid dual y-axes. Two scales on one plot invite false correlations; use two panels.
  • Remove chart junk: heavy gridlines, 3-D effects, shadows, backgrounds.
  • Size text so it is readable at the printed size: axis labels as large as the caption text.

Tables

  • Units in the column header, not in every cell.
  • Align numbers on the decimal point; use the same precision within a column.
  • Use few horizontal rules and no vertical ones (in LaTeX, the booktabs package).
  • Order rows by something meaningful (the baseline first, then by result), not by the order you ran them.
  • If you bold the best result, say so in the caption, and bold it only when the difference exceeds the noise.

Make figures reproducible

Generate every figure from logged data with a script kept in the repository, never by hand in a spreadsheet. When a reviewer asks "what happens at batch 4096?", you rerun one command. Name the figure file after the script that made it.

Refer to figures with a claim

"See Figure 2" makes the reader find the message. "Figure 2 shows that the gap grows with sequence length" tells them what to look for. The text and the caption should state the same takeaway in different words.

items.summary: Writing about GPUs, training and inference systems is mostly writing about code and machines. Code in prose is evidence: it shows the reader exactly what was done. Systems stories (optimisation worklogs, debugging sessions, incidents) are the form readers in this field read most, and the hardest to make useful.
items.title: 7. Code and systems narratives
items.html:
Writing about GPUs, training and inference systems is mostly writing about code and machines. Code in prose is evidence: it shows the reader exactly what was done. Systems stories (optimisation worklogs, debugging sessions, incidents) are the form readers in this field read most, and the hardest to make useful.

Code excerpts

  • Say what to look for, then show it. "The only change from the naive kernel is the mask on line 4, which keeps the last block from reading past the end:" then the code.
  • Show the smallest excerpt that carries the point. Usually 5–15 lines. Elide the rest with a comment (# ... load K and V as above ...).
  • Prefer runnable code in blogs and pseudocode in papers. Blog readers copy code; paper readers need the algorithm without your framework's boilerplate. In LaTeX, use an algorithm environment with numbered lines you can cite.
  • Make names in prose match names in code, in monospace: tl.atomic_add, max_queue_delay_microseconds.
  • Link to the full code at a fixed version: a commit hash or tag, not a branch that will change.
  • Commands must be copy-pasteable: full commands, required environment variables, and the expected output or the line to look for.

Explaining performance

A performance explanation names the bound, then shows the evidence for it:

  1. State the regime: memory-bound, compute-bound, latency-bound, launch-bound, or communication-bound.
  2. Show the arithmetic: bytes moved and FLOPs done, against the hardware's bandwidth and peak throughput (the roofline). "The kernel moves 3 GB in 0.42 ms, which is 7.1 TB/s against a measured copy ceiling of 6.6 TB/s: it is at the memory roof."
  3. Show the profile: the tool output (profiler trace, Nsight counters) that confirms the regime.
  4. Then explain the change and show the same evidence after it.

"It got faster because of better memory access" is a guess. "Coalesced loads cut device-memory (DRAM) transactions per request from 32 to 4, measured with Nsight Compute, and time fell in proportion" is an explanation.

The worklog

A worklog tells the story of an optimisation as a sequence of steps. Each step has the same five parts: what you expected, what you did, what you measured, what surprised you, and what you concluded. Simon Boehm's CUDA matmul worklog is the model: every step has a number, and the surprises are stated as surprises. Put a summary table of all steps at the top, so the reader knows where the story ends before it begins.

The postmortem

A postmortem explains a failure so that others can prevent the next one. Google's Site Reliability Engineering book describes the blameless postmortem: it assumes everyone acted reasonably given what they knew, and looks for the systemic causes. Structure (see templates/postmortem.md):

  1. Summary: what broke, the impact, the root cause, in three sentences.
  2. Impact: who or what was affected, for how long, measured.
  3. Timeline: timestamped observations, hypotheses and actions, including wrong hypotheses. Wrong turns are where the reader learns how to debug.
  4. Root cause and mechanism: why the failure happened, explained well enough that a reader could have predicted it.
  5. Contributing factors: what made it worse or slower to find.
  6. What went well, what did not.
  7. Action items: specific, owned, dated.

Debugging stories from your own work (a hang caused by an autotune key, a backend that misread arrays from a newer numpy) make excellent postmortems even when no production system was involved.

Design decision records

When you choose between designs, write down the context, the options considered, the decision, and its consequences, including the costs of the chosen option. One page is enough; many teams call this an architecture decision record (ADR). Six months later it answers "why did we do it this way?", and it is raw material for the design section of a paper.

Versions and environments

Systems results expire with versions. Always record the hardware, driver, CUDA, framework and library versions, and the exact commit of your code. A result without versions cannot be reproduced and, a year later, cannot be trusted.

items.summary: Drafting is getting the material out of your head; revision is making it usable by someone else's. Professionals spend more time revising than drafting. Revise in passes, from big to small: fixing sentences in a section you later delete wastes the work.
items.title: 8. Revision
items.html:
Drafting is getting the material out of your head; revision is making it usable by someone else's. Professionals spend more time revising than drafting. Revise in passes, from big to small: fixing sentences in a section you later delete wastes the work.

The passes, in order

PassQuestionTool
1. ArgumentIs the claim right-sized and fully supported?Claim–evidence table (D12)
2. StructureAre the points in the reader's order, one per paragraph?Reverse outline (D07)
3. ParagraphsDoes each first sentence state the point?Read first sentences only
4. SentencesActors as subjects, old before new, subject near verb?principles/03, read aloud (D44)
5. WordsFiller, hedges, vague claims, undefined terms?tw lint
6. Evidence detailsUnits, baselines, conditions, spread on every number?principles/04 checklist
7. FiguresOne message each; captions state it?principles/06
8. MechanicsSpelling, references, figure numbers, links, formattingSpell-checker, a final read

Get distance

You cannot see your own text while you still remember writing it. Create distance:

  • Cool off. Wait at least 24 hours before reviewing (tw review enforces it).
  • Change the medium. Print it, or read it on your phone, or in a different font.
  • Read it aloud. You will stumble exactly where a reader would.
  • Read it as your named reader. At each paragraph ask: would Priya know this word? Would she ask "compared with what?" here?

Cut

Most first drafts are 20–30% longer than they need to be. Cut in this order: sections the claim does not need, paragraphs that repeat, sentences that announce what the next sentence says ("In this section we will discuss..."), and words that do no work. Drill D43 makes this a habit. Cutting never removes a claim or a number; if it does, you cut the wrong thing.

Using feedback

  • Ask specific questions. "Is it clear?" gets "yes". "Where did you stop reading? What do you think the main claim is? Which number did you not trust?" gets data.
  • A reader's confusion is evidence; their suggested fix is a hypothesis. If a reader stumbled at paragraph 4, something is wrong at or before paragraph 4. Their proposed rewrite may not be the right repair.
  • Track changes you will make, in the review sheet's last column, and make them in one later session.
  • Thank reviewers, and tell them what you changed. It is how you get reviewed again.

Using AI tools

Use language models as reviewers, not writers. prompts/reviewer.md asks a model to quote your sentences and name problems without rewriting them. Three reasons:

  1. Learning. If a model rewrites, the model improves and you do not. The muscle you are building is the rewrite.
  2. Accuracy. Models produce fluent text that can be subtly wrong about your system, and fluent wrongness is the hardest kind to catch in review.
  3. Policy and voice. Many journals and conferences restrict AI-generated text and require disclosure of AI assistance; check the venue's policy before you submit. Editors and readers also recognise generic model prose, and it costs you credibility.

When is it done?

A piece is done when all of these are true:

  • The claim, reader and evidence lines at the top of the draft are true of the text.
  • The reverse outline is in the reader's order.
  • tw lint shows no unexplained fix items.
  • Every number has its five parts, traceable to a log.
  • One real reader has read it, and their confusion has been addressed.

Then ship it. Polishing past this point has fast-diminishing returns, and the next piece will teach you more.

items.title: Blog posts
items.html:
Reader: a practitioner who found your post through search, a feed or a colleague, and will leave at the first paragraph that wastes their time.

Decision they make: whether to use your idea, code or result in their own work.

Evidence bar: reproducible by the reader. Numbers with conditions, code they can run, links to the full source at a fixed commit.

Length: 1,200–3,000 words. Longer is fine if every section earns its place; the reader's patience is the budget.

What a good technical post does in its first 150 words

  1. Names the reader's problem in their terms ("Your data loader keeps the GPU waiting and you don't know why").
  2. States the result ("Six changes made the step 4× faster; two of them matter").
  3. Says what the reader will be able to do after reading.

Do not open with history, a definition of deep learning, or how you got interested in the topic.

Sub-genres

Each sub-genre has its own template in templates/.

Sub-genreShapeExemplars
Explainer (explainer.md)One concept, built from what the reader knows; a worked example; where the intuition breaksJay Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer; Chris Olah, Understanding LSTMs ; Lilian Weng's posts
Worklog (blog.md, worklog variant)Summary table first, then steps: expected → did → measured → surprised → concludedSimon Boehm, How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel; Horace He, Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles
Postmortem (postmortem.md)Summary, impact, timeline with wrong turns, mechanism, actionsCloudflare's incident write-ups; Google's Site Reliability Engineering book, chapter 15
Results post (blog.md)Claim, setup, results with baselines, limitations, how to reproduceLab and company engineering blogs (PyTorch, Hugging Face, Anyscale, vLLM)
Opinion or argumentThesis, the strongest counter-argument, evidence for each side, positionRich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson; Andrej Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks

Structure of a results or worklog post

  1. Title that states the finding: "Pinned memory halved our data-loader stalls", not "Notes on data loading".
  2. Summary: two or three sentences, with the main number and its baseline.
  3. Context: only enough for the reader to see why the problem matters. One paragraph.
  4. The body: in the reader's order (usually the explanation, then the evidence, then the detail).
  5. What did not work, briefly. Readers trust posts that report failures.
  6. Limitations: where the result stops applying (other hardware, shapes, scales).
  7. Reproduce it: commands, versions, link at a fixed commit.

Common failures

  • Chronological narrative that makes the reader wait for the result (fix: summary first; principles/02_structure.md).
  • Screenshot of a terminal in place of a table or a figure.
  • "X× faster" without baseline, conditions or variance (principles/04_numbers_and_evidence.md).
  • Copied code that does not run because an import, a version or a flag is missing.
  • Ending without a conclusion, or ending with "Thanks for reading". End with what the reader should do now.

Publishing

Publish on a site you control (GitHub Pages with Jekyll or Hugo, or your own domain) so links stay stable; cross-post to Medium, dev.to or Substack if you like, with a canonical link to the original. If the work was done for an employer, get approval first (publishing/process.md).

items.summary: In computer science, many results first appear at a conference; an extended journal version must usually add substantial new material (journals often expect around 30% new content, but policies vary; read the journal's policy on prior publication). Some journals, such as the Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), review on a rolling basis with no deadlines and focus on correctness more than perceived significance.
items.title: Journal articles
items.html:
Reader: an editor who chooses reviewers; two or three reviewers with more time than conference reviewers and higher expectations of completeness; later, researchers who want the definitive account of a piece of work.

Decision they make: accept, revise (major or minor), or reject, usually after one or more rounds of revision.

Evidence bar: complete. A journal article is expected to be the archival, self-contained account: full method, full experiments, full related work, limitations, and often proofs or extended analysis that a conference page limit excluded.

Length: usually longer than a conference paper (15–35 pages in many computing journals); check the journal's author guidelines.

How journals differ from conferences

ConferenceJournal
ReviewOne round, fixed deadline, short rebuttalSeveral rounds, no fixed deadline, full revisions
LengthStrict page limitLonger; completeness valued
SpeedMonthsMonths to more than a year
Response to reviewersRebuttal of one page or a word limitPoint-by-point response letter with every change
Typical contentNew resultNew result in full, or an extended version of a conference paper

In computer science, many results first appear at a conference; an extended journal version must usually add substantial new material (journals often expect around 30% new content, but policies vary; read the journal's policy on prior publication). Some journals, such as the Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), review on a rolling basis with no deadlines and focus on correctness more than perceived significance.

Structure

The structure follows the paper form (forms/paper.md), with more room:

  • A longer introduction that places the work in the field.
  • A full related-work section, often a survey in miniature.
  • Complete methods, including details relegated to appendices in the conference version.
  • Extended experiments: more workloads, more hardware, sensitivity analyses, failure cases.
  • A discussion section: implications, limitations, threats to validity.

The response letter

Revision rounds are where journal articles are won. The response letter (drill D42, templates/review.md for the reviewer side) follows a fixed pattern:

  1. Thank the reviewers once, briefly, at the start.
  2. Quote each comment in full, numbered (R1.1, R1.2, R2.1 ...).
  3. Respond to each: agree and describe the change with its location ("Section 5.2, new Figure 7"), or disagree politely with evidence.
  4. Quote or summarise the changed text, so the reviewer need not search for it.
  5. Never ignore a comment. If you did not change something, say why.

A reviewer who sees every point addressed specifically is far more likely to recommend acceptance in the next round.

Common failures

  • Submitting a conference paper unchanged with "extended" in the title.
  • Defensive responses that argue instead of improving the paper.
  • Changing the paper without saying where in the response.
  • Choosing a journal by prestige alone, rather than by whether its readers are the readers you want.

items.summary: A paper is a vehicle for a contribution: a new technique, a new analysis, a new system, a new measurement, or a new negative result. Before writing, state the contributions as a bulleted list of claims, each one testable (principles/01readerandclaim.md). Every section then supports one or more bullets. Simon Peyton Jones's talk How to Write a Great Research Paper puts it as: your paper conveys one ping, one clear idea.
items.title: Conference and workshop papers
items.html:
Reader: first, three to five reviewers with 20–50 papers each, reading yours in one or two sittings and deciding accept or reject; then researchers in your area deciding whether to cite, build on or compare against your work.

Decision they make: is this contribution new, correct, significant and well supported?

Evidence bar: the highest of the forms. Claims supported by experiments with fair baselines, ablations isolating each component, variance across runs, and enough detail to reproduce (ideally, an artifact that does).

Length: fixed by the venue (often 8–12 pages plus references for full papers, 4–6 for workshop papers). Check the current call for papers.

The contribution is everything

A paper is a vehicle for a contribution: a new technique, a new analysis, a new system, a new measurement, or a new negative result. Before writing, state the contributions as a bulleted list of claims, each one testable (principles/01_reader_and_claim.md). Every section then supports one or more bullets. Simon Peyton Jones's talk How to Write a Great Research Paper puts it as: your paper conveys one ping, one clear idea.

Structure (see templates/paper.md)

  1. Title: specific; often names the technique and the result.
  2. Abstract: problem, gap, approach, main result with a number, implication (drill D35, templates/abstract.md).
  3. Introduction (1–1.5 pages): the problem and why it matters, why existing approaches fall short, the key insight, the contributions as bullets, the main result. Many reviewers decide here.
  4. Background and motivation: only what the reader needs; often a measurement that motivates the design ("Figure 2: 61% of step time is spent waiting for input").
  5. Design / method: the idea first, then the mechanism, then the details. Figures of the architecture or algorithm.
  6. Implementation: what was built, on what, how large.
  7. Evaluation: questions first ("Does X improve throughput? Where does the gain come from? How does it scale?"), then experimental setup, then one subsection per question. Fair baselines, ablations, variance, limitations.
  8. Related work: grouped by approach, stating how yours differs from each group. Not a list of summaries.
  9. Conclusion: the contribution restated with the main evidence; one or two sentences of future work at most.

Systems papers versus ML papers

Systems venues (MLSys, OSDI, SOSP, ASPLOS, EuroSys) weigh design insight, real implementation and end-to-end measurements on realistic workloads. ML venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR) weigh novelty of method, theoretical grounding where available, and evaluation across standard benchmarks with statistical care. The same work can be framed for either; choose the framing, and the venue, by which contribution is strongest.

Common failures (from reviewers' complaints)

  • Unclear contribution: the reviewer cannot say in one sentence what is new.
  • Weak baselines: comparing an optimised method against an unoptimised baseline (principles/04_numbers_and_evidence.md, benchmarking crimes).
  • No ablation: the gain is shown but not attributed.
  • Overclaiming: "solves", "always", "general", supported by two models on one GPU.
  • Related work that hides the closest competitor: reviewers know it, and will ask.
  • Figures that cannot be read in print, or without colour.

Further reading

Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper (talk and slides); Jennifer Widom, Tips for Writing Technical Papers; Roy Levin and David Redell, An Evaluation of the Ninth SOSP Submissions; or, How (and How Not) to Write a Good Systems Paper (1983); Zachary Lipton and Jacob Steinhardt, Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship (2018).

items.summary: A white paper argues for a decision. A paper argues for knowledge; a blog shares practice. Every section of a white paper should help the reader decide, and the paper must state what it recommends. A white paper that only "explores the landscape" is a survey with a sales tone, and readers notice.
items.title: White papers
items.html:
Reader: a decision-maker (engineering director, architect, platform owner) and the technical lead they will forward it to. The first reads the executive summary; the second checks the evidence.

Decision they make: adopt, fund, change or stop something: a hardware purchase, a framework migration, a serving architecture, an investment in optimisation work.

Evidence bar: sufficient for the decision, honest about costs and risks. Measurements from your environment beat published benchmarks; cost per unit of work (dollars per million tokens, GPU-hours per training run) beats raw speed.

Length: 4–12 pages. The executive summary is one page at most.

What makes a white paper different

A white paper argues for a decision. A paper argues for knowledge; a blog shares practice. Every section of a white paper should help the reader decide, and the paper must state what it recommends. A white paper that only "explores the landscape" is a survey with a sales tone, and readers notice.

Structure (see templates/whitepaper.md)

  1. Executive summary. Problem, recommendation, expected benefit with a number, cost, main risk. Writable as five sentences; readable alone.
  2. The problem, in the reader's terms. Cost, time, risk or opportunity, measured: "Our training cluster is 35% GPU-busy; at current spend, the idle 65% costs ...".
  3. Options considered. Including doing nothing. Each option with its benefits, costs and risks, evaluated against the same criteria.
  4. Evidence. The measurements behind the comparison. Methods in enough detail for the technical lead to trust them; full detail in an appendix.
  5. Recommendation and plan. What to do, in what order, who does it, how long it takes, how success will be measured.
  6. Risks and mitigations. What could make the recommendation wrong, and what you will watch for.
  7. Appendices. Benchmark methods, configuration, raw data.

Writing for two readers

Write the executive summary and the section openings for the decision-maker: no jargon, numbers in business units, recommendation explicit. Write the evidence sections and appendices for the technical lead: full conditions, baselines, variance. Use the first sentence of each section for the decision-maker and the rest for the lead; that way, both can read the same document.

Common failures

  • No recommendation, or one hidden on page 9.
  • Options that are not real options, set up to lose to the preferred one. Decision-makers trust a paper that steelmans the alternatives.
  • Vendor-benchmark evidence in place of measurements on the reader's workload.
  • Speed without cost. A 2× faster option that costs 3× more per hour is slower per dollar.
  • Missing risks. Every recommendation has them; omitting them makes the reader find them, and then distrust everything else.

Exemplars

The NVIDIA and AMD architecture white papers (for describing hardware precisely), the Google TPU and Meta infrastructure papers (for evidence about systems decisions), and internal design documents in the style of Google's design docs (for options-and-trade-offs structure). Read them for structure, not for tone; a vendor's white paper argues for its product, and yours should argue for the reader's decision.

items.title: Seeds
items.html:
A seed is raw material for a piece: facts, numbers, sources, and the gaps in the evidence. It contains no prose and no angle. Finding the reader, the claim and the structure is the exercise. Seeds S1–S9 come from the GPU kernels course (../gpukernels); S10–S12 are for your own reinforcement learning (RL), training and math work.

All gpukernels numbers were measured on one NVIDIA GB200 (152 streaming multiprocessors, sm_100) with torch 2.12 and Triton 3.7, unless stated otherwise. Paths are relative to ../gpukernels/.

Before publishing any seed, close its evidence gaps: rerun with stated run counts, record variance, record versions and the commit. Lesson text is not a source; the scripts and logs are.

Seeds are notes for you, so they use the course's abbreviations freely. Your pieces must define them for their readers.

S1 · Shared-address atomics in the attention backward (week 5)

  • Backward pass with one shared bias table: 33,285 µs. With private per-program rows, then one sum(0): 474 µs.
  • Position table 256 entries, time table 32: 288 addresses in total, targeted by every program's BM·BN atomic adds per tile.
  • Same-address atomics serialise at the L2 slice that owns the line.
  • Autotuner needs reset_to_zero=["dpos_ptr", "dts_ptr"], or the accumulated gradients grow with each trial and the correctness check fails only on the first run.
  • Sources: course/07_hstu_attention_bwd.md, labs/07_hstu_attention_bwd/.
  • Evidence gaps: run count and spread for both timings; the batch shape used for the 33 ms number; a profiler counter that shows the serialisation (for example, atomic throughput or L2 stalls) rather than inferring it.

S2 · Making the baseline fair (week 3)

  • Dense PyTorch baseline is given pre-padded inputs (padded_inputs) so it is not charged for a Python padding loop; bf16 throughout.
  • Realistic batches are 45–52% padding.
  • Forward speedup: 10.4× (B=128, N≤200), 31.9× (B=64, N≤512, fused 121 µs), 12.9× (N≤2048). Peak memory at B=128, N≤200: 186 MB dense, 3 MB fused.
  • Forward+backward speedup: 20.4×, 31.7×, 6.5× at the same three shapes. Fused forward+backward peak memory 48 MB vs 996 MB dense (B=64, N≤512).
  • The reference's bias backward through advanced indexing took 1.26 s until it was replaced with bincount (TableGather in gk/hstu_ref.py): an unfair baseline that was fixed.
  • Sources: course/06_hstu_attention_fwd.md, course/07_hstu_attention_bwd.md, gk/hstu_ref.py.
  • Evidence gaps: run counts and spread; whether torch.compile or a FlashAttention-style dense baseline would narrow the gap; per-shape padding fractions.

S3 · The autotune key that hung training (week 7)

  • First training run hung for minutes per step.
  • The GEMM autotuner was keyed on M; in a jagged batch M is the token count, which changes every step, so every step re-ran autotuning (compile and benchmark every config).
  • Fix: key on M_BUCKET = triton.next_power_of_2(M).
  • Sources: course/04_matmul_silu.md, course/09_training.md, labs/04_matmul_silu/.
  • Evidence gaps: time per step before and after; number of configs; the number of distinct M values per epoch and per bucket.

S4 · Serving without Docker (week 7)

  • Triton Inference Server run from the binaries in the nvidia-pytriton wheel, with a matching Python 3.13 built for the backend stub (serving/setup_tritonserver.sh, logs/setup_tritonserver.log).
  • Every response failed with "output tensor shape does not match size of output". Copying arrays did not help; logging showed correct arrays. Cause: the stub is compiled against the numpy 1.x C ABI and misreads numpy 2 arrays. Fix: pass tensors via DLPack (serving/hstu_backend.py).
  • Correctness: served top-10 equals offline top-10 for 50 of 50 users.
  • Closed-loop load test, warm run: no batching 181 req/s (1 client), 270 req/s and p99 633 ms (128 clients); dynamic batching 3,940 req/s and p99 66 ms (128 clients), mean batch 48.4.
  • A first measurement showed a cold p99 of 1.56 s because warm-up had happened in a different instance.
  • Sources: course/10_serving.md, logs/client_warm.log, logs/client.log, logs/tritonserver.log.
  • Evidence gaps: duration of each load level; repeats; the hypotheses you tried in order, with timestamps if you can reconstruct them.

S5 · Where the training step's time goes (week 8)

  • Profiled step: 278 kernel launches in about 10 ms of wall time, about 2.3 ms of summed GPU kernel time (about 22% busy). Launch-bound.
  • Batch scaling: 0.40 M tokens/s at 32 users to 7.65 M tokens/s at 2,048 users (19×); step time flat (about 7.3–7.5 ms) from 32 to 512 users, 26.7 ms at 2,048.
  • CUDA graphs for inference: eager top-10 for one user 2,617 µs, graph replay 174 µs; gain shrinks to 7.5× at 64 users; identical results.
  • Start-up: cold 17.0 s; warm TRITON_CACHE_DIR 6.8 s; plus TRITON_CACHE_AUTOTUNING=1 2.7 s.
  • Top remaining GPU kernels are fp32 simt_sgemm and softmax backward of the loss: fp32 logits run on CUDA cores, not tensor cores.
  • Profiler and shared-GPU timings wobble by about ±30% between runs; the busy fraction is the stable signal.
  • Sources: course/11_system_opt.md, labs/11_system_opt/, logs/lab11.log.
  • Evidence gaps: cost per unit of work (GPU-hours per training run) for a white-paper reader; repeated runs; the effect of the bf16-logits fix, which has not been made yet.

S6 · Jagged fused attention for sequential recommenders (weeks 9–10)

  • Kernel: fused HSTU attention forward and backward on jagged batches (no padding, nothing N×N in HBM, causal block skipping). Speedups and memory as in S2; atomics as in S1.
  • Model quality on MovieLens-1M, HR@10 / NDCG@10: baseline 0.2353 / 0.1183; full softmax over 3,706 items + position embedding 0.2651 / 0.1460; 4 layers + full softmax + position embedding 0.2820 / 0.1557. Paper SASRec 0.2853 / 0.1603; paper HSTU about 0.31.
  • Training: 0.4 s per epoch with 2 layers.
  • End-to-end serving as in S4.
  • Sources: course/06–10, logs/exp_*.log, logs/train_ml1m_triton.log.
  • Evidence gaps: single runs per configuration, so seeds and spread are needed before any quality claim; a related-work survey (FlashAttention, jagged kernels in torchrec/fbgemm, the HSTU paper's own kernels); a second dataset; a second GPU.

S7 · A fused epilogue beats a faster GEMM (any week)

  • Skinny GEMM 65,536×1,024×256, bf16. cuBLAS: 925 TFLOP/s, 37 µs, but GEMM + separate SiLU takes 95 µs (the SiLU reads and writes 128 MiB each way).
  • Course step-2 kernel (TMA, persistent, warp-specialised): 763 TFLOP/s plain, but GEMM + fused SiLU in about 59 µs (1.6× faster than cuBLAS + SiLU).
  • Sources: course/04_matmul_silu.md, labs/04_matmul_silu/.
  • Evidence gaps: run counts; a cuBLASLt epilogue or torch.compile baseline, which can also fuse the activation.

S8 · Little's law and bytes in flight (any week; good for an explainer)

  • Vector add: Torch, Triton, Gluon and float4 CUDA reach about 7.1–7.2 TB/s; scalar CUDA about 4.1 TB/s; a plain copy 6.6 TB/s.
  • Gluon vector-width sweep: 7,208 / 7,174 / 7,133 / 7,134 GB/s for widths 1 / 2 / 4 / 8, because each thread already has 32 independent loads in flight.
  • Reduction: v2 2,362 GB/s (coalesced, one load in flight per thread), v3 5,823 GB/s (float4 and warp shuffles).
  • Sources: course/01_vector_add.md, course/05_cuda_reduction.md.
  • Evidence gaps: a measured memory latency for the GB200 (not "roughly 1 µs"); run counts.

S9 · A derivation (week 6)

Choose one:

  • The HSTU attention gradients: from Aij = 1N SiLU(α  qiᵀ kj + bij) for j ≤ i (zero otherwise) and O = AV, to dQ, dK, dV and the bias gradients; why recomputation beats storing A. Source: course/07_hstu_attention_bwd.md, gk/hstu_ref.py.
  • The policy-gradient theorem: from J(θ) = 𝔼τ ∼ πθ[R(τ)] to ∇θ J = 𝔼[∑t ∇θ log πθ(at ∣ st)  Gt]; why a baseline reduces variance without adding bias.
  • Little's law for memory: bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency, and what it predicts for S8.

S10 · Your reinforcement learning work

Fill in from your own experiments. Facts only.

  • Environment(s), algorithm(s), and what changed between runs:
  • Seeds per configuration, and the aggregate you report (mean, median, interquartile mean), with intervals:
  • Compute (GPU-hours) per run:
  • Logs:
  • Evidence gaps:

S11 · Your training work

  • Model, data, scale, hardware:
  • What you changed and what you measured (throughput, loss, quality), with baselines:
  • Logs:

items.title: Exemplars
items.html:
The weekly readings are listed in PROGRAM.md. This file collects them, plus books and a longer list for after week 12, grouped by what each one teaches. Verify links before relying on them; blog URLs move.

Books on writing (read one per quarter)

  • Joseph Williams and Joseph Bizup, Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace. The source of characters-as-subjects, actions-as-verbs and old-before-new. The most useful book on sentences.
  • Steven Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014). The curse of knowledge, and why "classic style" (showing the reader something you both can see) suits explanation.
  • William Zinsser, On Writing Well. Clutter, and how to cut it.
  • Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle. Conclusion first; grouping arguments. Written for consultants; essential for white papers.
  • Claus Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization (free online). Figures.
  • Edward Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Figures, with strong opinions.
  • Justin Zobel, Writing for Computer Science. Papers, end to end, including experiments and ethics.

Short guides (one sitting each)

  • George Gopen and Judith Swan, The Science of Scientific Writing (American Scientist, 1990).
  • Simon Peyton Jones, How to Write a Great Research Paper (talk and slides).
  • Paul Halmos, How to Write Mathematics (1970).
  • Donald Knuth, Tracy Larrabee and Paul Roberts, Mathematical Writing (1989).
  • Gernot Heiser, Systems Benchmarking Crimes.
  • Roy Levin and David Redell, How (and How Not) to Write a Good Systems Paper (1983).
  • Zachary Lipton and Jacob Steinhardt, Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship (2018).
  • Rishabh Agarwal et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice (NeurIPS 2021). On reporting reinforcement learning results.

By topic: read for the moves

GPUs and kernels

  • Simon Boehm, How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel for cuBLAS-like Performance: a Worklog. The worklog form.
  • Horace He, Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles. Explaining performance regimes to practitioners.
  • Tri Dao et al., FlashAttention (NeurIPS 2022). An argument from memory traffic, made in a paper.
  • Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson, Roofline (CACM 2009). A model explained so well that it became standard.

Training

  • Andrej Karpathy, A Recipe for Training Neural Networks (blog, 2019). Opinion grounded in practice.
  • Jared Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020). Presenting empirical laws with figures.
  • The Hugging Face Ultra-Scale Playbook (2025). Long-form systems explanation for practitioners.

Inference

  • Woosuk Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (SOSP 2023). A systems paper built on one clear analogy.

Reinforcement learning

  • Lilian Weng, Policy Gradient Algorithms (blog, 2018). Mathematics in a blog.
  • John Schulman et al., Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms (2017). A short paper with one idea.
  • Peter Henderson et al., Deep Reinforcement Learning that Matters (AAAI 2018). Evidence standards.

Explainers

  • Jay Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer. Figures carrying a mechanism.
  • Chris Olah, Understanding LSTM Networks . Building from what the reader knows.
  • Distill.pub articles (2016–2021). Interactive explanation at its best.

Systems narratives

  • Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 15 (postmortem culture).
  • Dan Luu, post-mortems (GitHub). A catalogue of real incidents.

You already read technical work for content. This protocol is for reading it for craft: seeing the decisions the author made so you can make them on purpose. Budget 45 minutes a week. Keep notes in journal/ with python tools/tw.py new reading SLUG, or in a plain file.

The protocol

  1. First pass, for content (10 min). Read normally. At the end, write the author's main claim in one sentence, from memory.
  2. Check (2 min). Find the sentence where the author states that claim. Where is it: title, first paragraph, end of the introduction, or nowhere? Did your sentence match theirs?
  3. Reverse outline (15 min). One line per paragraph (per section for a long paper): what does it do? Use verbs: claims, motivates, defines, shows evidence, concedes, compares, generalises. This is the author's structure laid bare.
  4. List the moves (10 min). Note three to five moves worth stealing. A move is a reusable technique, such as:
    • "Opens with a measurement that makes the problem feel urgent."
    • "States the result before the method."
    • "Concedes the strongest objection in its own paragraph, then answers it."
    • "Every figure caption is a full sentence stating the takeaway."
    • "Defines each symbol in the sentence that introduces it."
  5. Find one weakness (5 min). Where did you get lost, skim or doubt? Exemplars have faults too. Seeing them shows that the rules are about the reader, not about authority.
  6. Steal one move (3 min). Write which move you will use in this week's piece, and where.

What to notice, by form

FormLook for
BlogThe first 150 words; how code and prose alternate; how the post ends
White paperThe executive summary on its own; how options are compared; where cost appears
PaperThe abstract's five moves; the contributions list; how evaluation questions are framed; how related work positions the paper
Review / rebuttalWhich comments the authors addressed with new evidence, which with argument; tone

Imitation, once

Once in the twelve weeks, try the classic exercise of writers from Benjamin Franklin onwards. Take one paragraph you admire, note its moves in a list, close the source, and write a paragraph on your own topic that makes the same moves. Then compare. You are copying the structure, never the words.

items.summary: If the work was done for an employer, find out before drafting:
items.title: From draft to published
items.html:
Before you write: permissions

If the work was done for an employer, find out before drafting:

  • Who approves external publication, and how long approval takes (often weeks). Many companies require legal, IP (intellectual property) and security review of anything public, including blogs.
  • Whether a patent filing must come first. Public disclosure can destroy patent rights in many jurisdictions.
  • What you may disclose: model sizes, hardware counts, customer data, internal names, numbers that reveal capacity or cost.
  • Whether your name, your team's or the company's goes on it, and which affiliation to list.

Side projects on your own time and hardware (such as the GPU kernels course) usually avoid most of this, but check your employment agreement.

Blog posts

  1. Draft, cool off, self-review (tw review), outside review (a colleague and prompts/reviewer.md).
  2. Check every number against its log, every command by running it, every link by clicking it.
  3. Get approval if required.
  4. Publish on a site you control; cross-post with a canonical link if you want reach.
  5. Share where your readers are, with the claim in the post text, not "new blog post!".

Preprints (arXiv)

  • arXiv accepts preprints in computer science after a light moderation check. First-time submitters in a category may need an endorsement from an existing author.
  • Most ML venues allow arXiv preprints of submitted work; some venues restrict publicising a paper during anonymous review. Check the venue's anonymity policy before posting or promoting.
  • Choose the licence deliberately; it cannot be made more restrictive later.
  • Post a new version when the paper changes materially, and keep the version history clean.

Conference submission

  1. Read the call for papers completely: page limit, template, anonymity rules, supplementary material, artifact policy, AI-use policy, conflicts of interest.
  2. Use the official template from the start; never fight formatting the night before.
  3. Anonymise if the venue is double-blind: no names, no identifying URLs, cite your own prior work in the third person.
  4. Submit an abstract if the venue requires one before the paper deadline.
  5. Rebuttal: you may get a short window to answer reviews. Answer the comments that could change a decision first; be brief, specific and courteous; offer new results only if you have them (drill D42).
  6. Camera-ready: address the reviewers' requests, de-anonymise, and meet the final formatting checks.
  7. Artifact evaluation (optional at many systems venues): package code, data and scripts so a committee can reproduce the main results; badges signal reproducibility to readers.

Journal submission

  1. Read the author guidelines and the policy on prior publication (an extended conference paper usually needs substantial new material).
  2. Write a cover letter: what the paper contributes, why it fits the journal, and how it differs from any prior version.
  3. Suggest reviewers if invited, and declare conflicts.
  4. Expect one or more rounds of revision: major revision, minor revision, then acceptance (or rejection at any stage).
  5. For each round, write a response letter (see forms/journal.md): every comment quoted, answered, and located in the revised text.

Rejection

Most papers are rejected at least once; acceptance rates at top venues are often around 20–25%. Treat a rejection as a free, expert review. Within a week:

  1. Read the reviews once, then wait a day.
  2. Sort the comments: misunderstandings (fix the writing), missing evidence (run the experiment), disagreements about significance (reframe, or choose a different venue).
  3. Revise before resubmitting. Reviewers at the next venue may include the same people.

AI tools and disclosure

Policies on the use of AI writing tools differ across publishers and venues and are changing. Common patterns: language models cannot be listed as authors; substantive use of AI-generated text must be disclosed; reviewers must not upload submissions they review to AI tools. Read the current policy of the specific venue. This program uses AI only as a critic (prompts/reviewer.md), so your text remains your own writing.
