items.title: Venues
items.html:
Where work on GPUs, training, inference, reinforcement learning, systems and their mathematics is published. Deadlines, page limits and policies change every year: always read the current call for papers and author guidelines. This file deliberately gives no dates.

Choose a venue by its readers first: who do you want to read the work, and where do they read?

Conferences: machine learning systems, architecture, high-performance computing

VenueReaders and fit
MLSysML systems: training and inference systems, compilers, kernels, hardware for ML
ASPLOSArchitecture, programming languages and operating systems together; accelerators, compilers
ISCA, MICRO, HPCAComputer architecture; GPU and accelerator microarchitecture
SC (Supercomputing)High-performance computing; large-scale training, communication, performance analysis
PPoPPParallel programming: GPU algorithms, concurrency, performance
CGOCode generation and optimisation; compilers such as Triton and those built on Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)

Conferences: operating systems and distributed systems

VenueReaders and fit
OSDI, SOSPTop systems venues; serving systems, cluster schedulers, storage for ML
EuroSys, USENIX ATCSystems with strong implementation and evaluation
NSDINetworked and distributed systems; collective communication, datacentre networking

Conferences: machine learning and reinforcement learning

VenueReaders and fit
NeurIPS, ICML, ICLRMethods, theory and empirical ML; each has workshops (often 4–8 pages, some non-archival) that suit early work
RLC (Reinforcement Learning Conference)Reinforcement learning specifically
AAMASAgents and multi-agent systems, including multi-agent reinforcement learning
AISTATS, UAIStatistical and probabilistic ML, theory

Conferences: recommender systems, data mining, information retrieval

VenueReaders and fit
RecSysRecommender systems; industry tracks welcome systems and deployment papers
KDDData mining; applied data science track for production work
WWW (The Web Conference), WSDMWeb-scale systems and mining
SIGIR, CIKMRetrieval, ranking, applied information systems

Journals

JournalReaders and fit
JMLRMachine learning, archival; no page limit
TMLRMachine learning, rolling submission; reviews for correctness and evidence more than perceived significance
IEEE TPDSParallel and distributed systems
ACM TACOArchitecture and code optimisation
ACM TOCSComputer systems
ACM TORSRecommender systems
IEEE TPAMIPattern analysis and machine intelligence
IEEE MicroArchitecture and hardware, for a broader engineering audience; shorter articles
Communications of the ACM (CACM)Broad computing audience; research highlights and practice articles

Practitioner venues

  • ACM Queue: practitioners writing for practitioners; peer-reviewed articles on practice.
  • Company and lab engineering blogs: often the highest-readership venue for systems work.
  • arXiv: not a venue but a preprint server; see process.md.
  • Workshops at systems conferences (for example, workshops on ML systems co-located with ASPLOS, ISCA or MLSys): fast feedback on early work.

Choosing

  1. Find five papers you would cite, and note where they appeared. Your readers are there.
  2. Read three papers from the last edition of the venue: is your contribution the kind they publish?
  3. Match the evidence bar: architecture venues expect simulation or hardware evidence; systems venues expect a real implementation and end-to-end evaluation; ML venues expect benchmarks with statistical care.
  4. Check whether the venue offers artifact evaluation (many systems venues do), and plan for it from the start.

items.title: Reviewer prompt
items.html:
Paste everything between the lines into a strong language model, followed by your draft. Use it after your own cool-off review, never instead of it. The prompt forbids rewriting on purpose: if the model rewrites your sentences, it gets the practice and you do not.

If the model rewrites anyway, discard that comment and tell it: "Do not rewrite. Quote and diagnose only."

You are a demanding but fair technical editor reviewing a draft. Your job is to make the writer better, not to make this draft better yourself.

Context:

  • Form: [blog / explainer / white paper / paper / postmortem / abstract]
  • Intended reader: [paste the Reader line from the top of the draft]
  • Intended claim: [paste the Claim line]

Rules:

  1. Do not rewrite any sentence, and do not supply replacement wording. For each problem, quote the exact words (at most 25), name the problem, and explain why it would hurt the intended reader. You may say what kind of change is needed ("state the baseline", "move the result before the method") but not write the change.
  2. Prioritise in this order: argument (is the claim supported and right-sized?), structure (are points in the reader's order?), evidence (numbers with baselines, conditions and variance; fair comparisons), clarity (sentences, terms, definitions), mechanics. Do not comment on mechanics if there are problems higher up.
  3. Give at most 10 comments, most important first. Fewer is fine.
  4. For every number, check: unit, baseline, conditions, spread, source. Flag any that are missing.
  1. Flag any claim stronger than its evidence (for example "always", "solves", "significantly" without a test).
  2. Do not praise. Do not summarise the draft back.
  3. End with:
    • Main claim as I understood it: one sentence in your words. (The writer will compare it with what they intended.)
    • The question the intended reader would most want answered that the draft does not answer.

Draft:

[paste draft]

After the review

  1. Compare the model's "main claim as I understood it" with your Claim line. If they differ, fix the draft's argument before anything else.
  2. For each comment, decide: agree, disagree (note why), or unsure (ask a human reader).
  3. Make the changes yourself, in a later session. Record them in the last column of your review sheet.
  4. Remember: a model's confusion is evidence that something is unclear; it is not proof, and its diagnosis may be wrong. Your human reader outranks it.
